title: OCI Cricketers' Fight to Play in India Now Waits on the Centre's Stand
excerpt: Twelve OCI-cardholding youngsters have challenged the BCCI's Indian-passport rule in the Bombay High Court. The court has sought the Central Government's stand, saying any order could have wide ramifications.
body:
• Twelve young cricketers who hold Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cards are challenging the BCCI rule that only Indian passport holders may play in its domestic tournaments.
  • The Bombay High Court has made the Central Government a party to the case, saying an order could have wide ramifications, and sought the Centre's affidavit; the matter was listed for October 14.
  • The BCCI's position is that domestic cricket feeds the national team, and only Indian citizens can represent India — so OCI cardholders become eligible only if they take Indian citizenship.
  • For diaspora families, the practical rule today is unchanged: an OCI card lets a child live and study in India, but it does not open the door to BCCI domestic cricket.

A group of twelve young cricketers has taken Indian cricket's governing body to court over a question that reaches far beyond sport: what, exactly, does an Overseas Citizen of India card entitle its holder to do? The petitioners — Kavin Kartik and eleven minors — were born abroad and hold the citizenship of their birth countries. Their parents are Indian nationals, the children hold OCI cards, and they live in India, where they study and play cricket. A BCCI rule now bars them from the domestic game entirely.

The rule being challenged

The dispute began with a BCCI resolution, adopted in December 2023 and applied from 2024, under which only players holding an Indian passport may take part in tournaments organised by the board or its affiliates. Foreign citizens — including OCI and Person of Indian Origin cardholders who had previously been allowed to play — were made ineligible. The board's stated purpose is to protect opportunities for Indian nationals in a system that feeds selection for the national team.

The petitioners argue the change is arbitrary and discriminatory, and violates the equality guarantee in Article 14 of the Constitution. Their counsel have asked what happens to the rights and development of children who have trained in India for years if they are suddenly shut out of competitive cricket. The BCCI has told the court its policy was a collective decision, that only Indian nationals can be selected to represent the country internationally, and that OCI cardholders were informed they would become eligible if they obtained Indian citizenship.

What the court has said so far

The case has moved through several benches without a final answer. At a hearing in July, the court suggested the young players consider playing for their country of citizenship, or taking Indian citizenship if they want to play for India. In September 2025, a different bench refused interim relief, holding that the petitioners had not made out a case of manifest arbitrariness and that letting OCI players into domestic tournaments would come at the cost of Indian nationals.

Most recently, on September 10, a bench led by Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi directed the petitioners to make the Central Government a party, observing that any order could have wide ramifications and that the court first needed the government's stand — including whether the Centre's position is that no OCI holder can represent the country. The government was ordered to file its affidavit, and the matter was listed for October 14. No final order has been reported.

Why this matters beyond cricket

The mechanism at the heart of the case is simple but often misunderstood in diaspora families. An OCI card is a lifelong visa and residence status for foreign citizens of Indian origin. It is not citizenship: India does not permit dual citizenship, and an OCI holder remains a foreign national in Indian law, without a vote and, under the BCCI's rule, without access to domestic cricket. The petitioners' families face a stark version of that trade-off — a child who wants a domestic cricket career in India must, on the board's current position, surrender a foreign passport and take Indian citizenship, a decision with lifelong consequences that has to be made in the teenage years, when cricket careers are decided.

The court's insistence on hearing the Centre reflects the same stakes. A ruling for the cricketers would raise questions for every sport federation that restricts domestic competition to citizens, and for other fields where OCI holders seek treatment equal to citizens. A ruling for the BCCI would settle the opposite principle: that in Indian law, the line between citizen and OCI holder is a real one, and institutions may enforce it.

What happens next

The Central Government's affidavit is the next substantive step, followed by a full hearing on the petitions, including the July observations reported by Live Law. Until a final order is passed, the passport rule stands and the twelve petitioners remain outside BCCI tournaments. For OCI families weighing a move to India for a child's sporting career, the operative advice is unchanged: read the eligibility rule of the relevant federation before the move, not after it.
